analogy.p: Imagine an acid as a coach full of passengers (hydrogen ions) and a driver (the negative ion, such as chloride). A reactive metal is a bouncer who swaps places with the passengers, sending them off as hydrogen gas while he becomes part of the team (the salt). A base or carbonate is a drop-off station that takes the passengers into water, sometimes releasing a puff of carbon dioxide. This maps correctly because the negative ion stays the same and only the positive part changes. It breaks down because ions are charged particles in solution and are not carried by a vehicle, and reactions are driven by the particles colliding rather than by deliberate swapping.
analogy.t: The acid as a team of hydrogen 'passengers'

bullets: **Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen** (only for metals more reactive than hydrogen).
**Acid + base (metal oxide or metal hydroxide) → salt + water**. This is a neutralisation reaction.
**Acid + alkali (soluble metal hydroxide) → salt + water**. Alkalis are a special group of bases that dissolve in water.
**Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide**.
In every case the **acid supplies the negative part of the salt** and the **metal/base supplies the positive part**.
Common lab acids: hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3), all used dilute at GCSE.
core.h: The three reaction patterns to learn
core.p: Acids are substances that release hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water, and this single fact explains all of their typical reactions. At GCSE there are three patterns you must be able to recall, write equations for and apply to any acid and any metal, base or carbonate. In each pattern the products always include a **salt**, which is a compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal (or ammonium) ion. Learning the patterns as general word equations lets you answer unfamiliar examples quickly.

bullets: **Hydrochloric acid** gives **chlorides** (e.g. magnesium chloride, MgCl2).
**Sulfuric acid** gives **sulfates** (e.g. copper sulfate, CuSO4). Spell it 'sulfate', not 'sulphate'.
**Nitric acid** gives **nitrates** (e.g. sodium nitrate, NaNO3).
The first word is the metal: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid gives **magnesium** chloride; zinc carbonate + sulfuric acid gives **zinc** sulfate.
Example: copper(II) oxide + sulfuric acid → copper(II) sulfate + water.
Sodium hydroxide + nitric acid → sodium nitrate + water.
core.h: Naming salts: which acid and which positive ion
core.p: The name of a salt has two parts. The **first word** comes from the metal in the metal, base, alkali or carbonate (the positive ion), and the **second word** comes from the acid used (the negative ion). This is exactly what the specification says: the salt produced depends on the acid used and on the positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate. Being able to name salts is a very frequent 1-2 mark question, and getting the endings right is easy marks.

bullets: Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen: **Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2**.
Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen: **Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2**.
Iron + hydrochloric acid → iron(II) chloride + hydrogen: **Fe + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2** (pale green solution).
Aluminium: **2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2**. Aluminium reacts slowly at first because of its protective layer of aluminium oxide, even though it is quite high in the series.
Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid because it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
Very reactive metals (potassium, sodium, lithium) react explosively with acid, so they are **never** used in school practicals.
core.p: Reactive metals react with dilute acids to give a salt and hydrogen gas. The reaction happens because the metal atoms are able to give electrons to the hydrogen ions in the acid, so hydrogen gas bubbles off and the metal ions form the salt with the negative ion of the acid. Only metals **above hydrogen in the reactivity series** react, and the rate of reaction increases with reactivity, which is how we compare reactivity in the lab. Unreactive metals such as copper, silver and gold show no reaction at all.

bullets: Order of reactivity from observation: **magnesium (rapid fizzing) > zinc (steady) > iron (slow)**; copper shows no reaction.
**Control variables:** same volume and concentration of acid, same temperature, same mass or surface area of metal (e.g. same-sized ribbon or powder).
**Independent variable:** type of metal. **Dependent variable:** rate of hydrogen production (bubbles per minute, volume per time) or temperature rise.
The reaction is **exothermic**, so the temperature rises. More reactive metals give a bigger and faster temperature rise.
A steeper line on a graph of volume of H2 against time means a faster reaction; the line levels off when the limiting reactant is used up.
Safety: eye protection; hydrogen is flammable so avoid naked flames; wear gloves with stronger acid; dilute acid is an irritant.
core.p: A simple practical compares how quickly different metals react with the same dilute acid. The faster the fizzing, the more reactive the metal. You can make this quantitative by measuring the volume of hydrogen collected in a gas syringe against time, or by measuring the temperature rise. Because the question is whether the metal is reactive, you must keep other factors the same so the test is fair. This links to rates of reaction because the steepness of the volume-time graph is the rate.

bullets: Test: lit splint at the mouth of the tube; positive result: **squeaky pop**.
The pop is caused by the combustion 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.
Collect hydrogen by displacement of water or in a gas syringe; the gas is insoluble in water.
Do not confuse with oxygen (relights a glowing splint) or carbon dioxide (limewater turns milky).
A 'squeaky pop' mark scheme answer needs both the lit splint and the sound.
Hydrogen is also the fuel in hydrogen fuel cells, linking to energy topics.
core.p: You must be able to identify the gas given off. Hydrogen is a colourless, odourless gas that is less dense than air and explosively flammable. The standard test is to hold a **lit splint** at the mouth of a test tube of the gas. A positive result is a **squeaky pop**, which is the sound of hydrogen burning rapidly with oxygen from the air to form water. Because the gas is lighter than air, collect it in an upturned tube or in a gas syringe rather than an open container.

bullets: Ionic equation: **Mg + 2H+ → Mg2+ + H2**.
Half equations: **Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-** (oxidation) and **2H+ + 2e- → H2** (reduction).
For zinc: Zn + 2H+ → Zn2+ + H2. For iron: Fe + 2H+ → Fe2+ + H2 (iron forms Fe2+ here, not Fe3+).
The reactivity series is a series of how easily a metal loses electrons, so metals above hydrogen can reduce H+ and those below cannot.
Aluminium: 2Al + 6H+ → 2Al3+ + 3H2 (3 electrons lost per atom).
Chloride, sulfate and nitrate ions are spectators and left out of ionic equations.
core.h: The metal-acid reaction as oxidation and reduction (Higher tier)
core.p: At Higher tier you should be able to explain the metal-acid reaction in terms of electron transfer. The metal atoms **lose electrons** and become positive ions: this is **oxidation**. The hydrogen ions in the acid **gain electrons** and form hydrogen molecules: this is **reduction**. The other ions in the acid (chloride, sulfate or nitrate) do not change and are **spectator ions**, which is why the ionic equation is shorter than the full symbol equation. This is a typical 'explain in terms of electrons' question.

bullets: Acid + metal oxide → salt + water: **CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O** (black solid dissolves, solution turns blue).
**MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O**; **ZnO + 2HNO3 → Zn(NO3)2 + H2O**.
Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water: **NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O**; **Ca(OH)2 + 2HNO3 → Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O**.
All alkalis are bases, but **not all bases are alkalis**: copper(II) oxide and iron(III) hydroxide are bases that do not dissolve in water.
Insoluble bases cannot be added until the indicator changes; they are added in excess and the leftover solid is filtered off (link to making salts).
Neutralisation is **exothermic**: the temperature of the mixture rises.
core.h: Acids reacting with bases and alkalis (neutralisation)
core.p: A **base** is a substance that neutralises an acid; bases include metal oxides and metal hydroxides. An **alkali** is a base that dissolves in water, forming hydroxide ions (OH-); examples are sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide solution. When an acid reacts with a base, the hydrogen ions are used up and a salt and water form, which is why the pH moves towards 7. This is **neutralisation**, and it is not a redox reaction because no electrons are transferred.

bullets: Acid + alkali: **H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l)**.
Acid + metal oxide: **2H+(aq) + O2-(s) → H2O(l)** (in the solid oxide; the metal ion goes into solution).
Example, MgO + 2H+ → Mg2+ + H2O.
Acid + carbonate: **2H+ + CO3 2- → H2O + CO2**.
Spectator ions, e.g. Na+ and Cl- in NaOH + HCl, are present before and after unchanged.
If the pH of the final mixture is 7, the amounts of H+ and OH- were exactly equal (equivalent).
core.h: The ionic equation for neutralisation (Higher tier)
core.p: In every neutralisation of an acid with an alkali the real change is the same: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join to make water. The metal and non-metal ions are spectators, which explains why all strong acid and alkali neutralisations release a similar amount of energy. You should be able to write this equation with state symbols. For a metal oxide, the oxide ion takes two hydrogen ions to form water, so the balancing is different.

bullets: **CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2** (marble chips with hydrochloric acid).
**Na2CO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + H2O + CO2**.
**CuCO3 + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O + CO2** (green solid dissolves to give a blue solution).
**ZnCO3 + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2O + CO2**.
Marble chips with sulfuric acid slow down as the sparingly soluble calcium sulfate forms a coating on the surface of the chips.
The gas can be collected over water or with a gas syringe and tested with limewater.
core.p: Metal carbonates react with acids to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The carbonate ion accepts hydrogen ions to form carbonic acid, which immediately breaks down into water and carbon dioxide gas, so the mixture **fizzes (effervescence)**. The solid carbonate gradually disappears as it dissolves, and the reaction mixture may warm up slightly. This reaction is the basis of limescale removal and of antacid tablets that contain carbonates.

bullets: Test: bubble the gas through **limewater**; positive result: limewater turns **milky/cloudy white**.
Equation: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O.
Method: connect a delivery tube from the reaction flask into a test tube of limewater, putting the end of the tube under the surface.
Distinguish from hydrogen (squeaky pop) and oxygen (relights a glowing splint).
Acids with carbonates: fizzing is the observation; the identity of the gas needs the limewater test.
Do not say 'turns white' without 'milky/cloudy' - use the mark scheme wording.
core.p: Carbon dioxide is identified using **limewater**, which is a solution of calcium hydroxide. When carbon dioxide is bubbled through, it reacts with the calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which makes the solution turn **milky (cloudy)**. This is a precipitation reaction and a very reliable test. If you carry on bubbling the gas, the milkiness can disappear again as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms, but this is beyond the spec.

bullets: Metal + acid: **bubbles/fizzing**, the metal gets smaller and disappears, the test tube warms up (exothermic).
Metal oxide + acid: **solid dissolves**, no gas; copper oxide gives a **blue** solution (needs warming).
Alkali + acid: no visible change, so use **an indicator** or pH probe to see the end-point (neutralisation).
Carbonate + acid: **fizzing**, solid disappears; gas turns limewater milky.
Fe + acid: pale green solution (Fe2+); Cu compounds: blue solution; Zn, Mg, Na compounds: colourless.
Temperature rise in all three cases shows the reactions are **exothermic**.
core.h: Observations: how to describe each reaction
core.p: Examiners often ask what you would see, so link each reaction type to its observations. Metals give effervescence and the metal gets smaller; bases such as copper oxide dissolve with a colour change and no fizzing; carbonates fizz and dissolve. Colours often tell you the metal ion present: copper(II) salts are blue, iron(II) salts pale green and most other salts colourless. Always write the observation, not just the products.

bullets: Moles = mass (g) / Mr, and gas volume (dm3) = moles × 24 at rtp.
Example: 0.12 g Mg (Ar 24) with excess HCl: moles Mg = 0.12/24 = 0.005; ratio 1:1 gives 0.005 mol H2; volume = 0.005 × 24 = 0.12 dm3 = **120 cm3**.
Example: 5.0 g CaCO3 (Mr 100) with excess HCl: 0.05 mol CaCO3 gives 0.05 mol CO2 = 1.2 dm3.
Check the ratio: 2HCl needed per CaCO3, so excess acid means the carbonate is the limiting reactant.
In practical gas syringe experiments the volume of gas is read in cm3.
Limiting reactant: the one used up first, which decides the amount of product.
core.h: Using the equations: calculations and moles
core.p: These equations are the basis for calculations on mass and gas volume. Balance the equation first, convert the given mass to moles, use the ratio in the equation, then convert back to mass or volume. For gases at room temperature and pressure (rtp), one mole of any gas occupies **24 dm3** (24 000 cm3). The same method as any reacting-masses question applies; the new element is knowing the products of acid reactions.

bullets: **Indigestion tablets** contain bases such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate, which neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
**Farmers** add lime (calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide or calcium carbonate) to acidic soils to raise the pH.
**Limescale removal**: calcium carbonate deposits react with acids such as citric or hydrochloric acid and fizz away.
**Acid rain** reacts with limestone and marble (calcium carbonate), eroding statues and buildings.
**Factories** neutralise acidic waste with an alkali (or base) before release.
The same reactions are the basis for preparing soluble salts in the laboratory (required practical).
core.h: Applications of acid reactions in everyday life
core.p: These reactions are not just exam material: they explain how antacids work, how soils are treated, how limescale is removed, and why acid rain damages limestone buildings. Neutralisation with a carbonate or base is used when the aim is to raise pH safely. Understanding the particles also explains why chemicals such as lime are spread on fields or lakes to counteract acidity. Questions often ask you to evaluate or apply, so be able to link the equation to the use.

bullets: **Redox:** metal + acid is redox (metal oxidised, H+ reduced). Acid + base and acid + carbonate are **not** redox: no electron transfer.
**Strong vs weak acids:** the same type of products form, but weak acids ionise only partially so the rate is slower for the same concentration.
**Rates of reaction:** increasing concentration, temperature, surface area (powder rather than lump) or using a catalyst changes the rate of acid-metal and acid-carbonate reactions.
**Making salts:** soluble salts from acid + insoluble base/metal/carbonate, filtering off excess solid, then crystallising.
**Titration:** acid + alkali with an indicator to find concentrations.
**Conservation of mass:** the mass of the flask decreases when gas escapes, but total mass is conserved if the gas is included.
core.h: Linking to other topics and extension ideas
core.p: This topic links directly to the reactivity series, oxidation and reduction, preparing salts, the pH scale and rates of reaction. The metal-acid reaction is evidence for the reactivity series: metals that fizz are above hydrogen. Neutralisation links to titration calculations, and the carbonate reaction links to thermal decomposition and tests for gases. Higher tier students should also be ready to state which reactions are redox and which are not.

exam: **Recall the general equations** (1-2 marks): 'acid + metal → salt + hydrogen', 'acid + base → salt + water', 'acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide'.
**Name the salt** (1 mark): first word from the metal, second word from the acid: hydrochloric = chloride, sulfuric = sulfate, nitric = nitrate.
**Word equation** (1-2 marks): write the reactants and products with correct names; mark scheme accepts any correct order of products.
**Balanced symbol equation** (2 marks): correct formulae (1) then balancing (1). Check charges: Mg2+ with Cl- needs two chlorides.
**State the test and result** (2 marks): hydrogen - lit splint, squeaky pop; carbon dioxide - limewater turns milky.
**Ionic equations** (Higher, 1-2 marks): Mg + 2H+ → Mg2+ + H2; H+ + OH- → H2O. Spectator ions are not included.
**Oxidation/reduction** (Higher, 2 marks): 'Magnesium atoms lose electrons (oxidised); hydrogen ions gain electrons (reduced)'.
**Compare reactivity** (2-3 marks): fizzing rate or volume of gas against time, keeping acid concentration, volume, temperature and metal surface area the same.
**Graphs of gas volume against time**: steeper means faster; the plateau shows the reaction has finished and the final volume depends on the amount of limiting reactant.
**Calculation questions** (3-4 marks): balanced equation, moles, ratio, then volume using 24 dm3/mol; show working and include units.
**6-mark questions**: describe a method, identify the gas and test, give the equation and explain the observations including temperature change.

mistakes.r: Acid + metal gives a salt and HYDROGEN. Water is formed with bases and carbonates.
mistakes.w: Acid + metal gives a salt and water.

mistakes.r: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so there is no reaction.
mistakes.w: Copper reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to give hydrogen.

mistakes.r: Sulfuric acid makes sulfates; hydrochloric acid makes chlorides; nitric acid makes nitrates.
mistakes.w: Sulfuric acid makes sulphide salts / hydrochloric makes chlorine.

mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky (cloudy). State both the gas and the observation.
mistakes.w: Limewater turns white / cloudy (no mention of gas).

mistakes.r: Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint; oxygen relights a glowing splint.
An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Many bases (e.g. copper oxide) are insoluble.
Acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Magnesium chloride is MgCl2; balance: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2.
Chloride ions are spectators; the metal is oxidised and the H+ ions are reduced.
mistakes.w: In the metal-acid reaction the chloride ions are oxidised.

summary: AQA 4.4.2 expects you to know that acids react with metals to make a salt and hydrogen, with bases and alkalis (metal oxides and hydroxides) to make a salt and water, and with metal carbonates to make a salt, water and carbon dioxide. You must name the salt formed, write word, symbol and ionic equations, describe the gas tests, and (Higher tier) explain the metal-acid reaction as oxidation and reduction. It matters because these three reaction types underpin salt preparation, neutralisation in medicine and agriculture, and the reactivity series.

terms.d: A substance that forms hydrogen ions (H+) when dissolved in water; its pH is below 7.
A substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water; includes metal oxides and hydroxides.
A base that is soluble in water and forms hydroxide ions (OH-) in solution.
A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
A reaction between an acid and a base or alkali that forms a salt and water (H+ + OH- → H2O).
Fizzing caused by bubbles of gas released from a liquid.
The salt produced from hydrochloric acid.
The salt produced from sulfuric acid.
The salt produced from nitric acid.
A list of metals in order of how readily they react; metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids.
A solution of calcium hydroxide used to test for carbon dioxide; it turns milky.
The sound given when a lit splint is put into hydrogen; the test for hydrogen.
An ion that is unchanged by the reaction and does not appear in the ionic equation.
An equation showing only the ions or particles that change in a reaction.
Loss of electrons (Higher tier); the metal atoms are oxidised when they react with acid.
Gain of electrons (Higher tier); hydrogen ions are reduced to hydrogen gas.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.

worked.ans: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2. Hydrogen is identified with a lit splint, which makes a squeaky pop.
worked.q: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of zinc with dilute sulfuric acid and describe the test for the gas formed. (3 marks)
steps: Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen.
Formulae: Zn, H2SO4, ZnSO4 (Zn2+ and SO4 2-), H2. Equation is already balanced: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2.
Test: lit splint at the mouth of the tube; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop.

worked.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid. (a) Name the products. (b) Calculate the volume of gas produced from 5.0 g of calcium carbonate. Ar: Ca 40, C 12, O 16; 1 mole of gas = 24 dm3. (4 marks)
steps: Products: calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.
Ratio 1 CaCO3 : 1 CO2 so moles CO2 = 0.050.

worked.ans: Model answer: Magnesium atoms lose two electrons and are oxidised to Mg2+. The H+ ions from the acid gain these electrons and are reduced to hydrogen gas. The chloride ions are unchanged (spectators).
worked.q: Explain, in terms of electrons, what happens when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. (4 marks, Higher tier)
steps: Mark 1: magnesium atoms lose two electrons to form Mg2+ ions (Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-).
Mark 2: this is oxidation because it is loss of electrons.
Mark 3: hydrogen ions gain electrons to form hydrogen molecules (2H+ + 2e- → H2).
Mark 4: this is reduction because it is gain of electrons; the chloride ions are spectator ions.
